parsed.explanation: Combined regime: a protective sub-unit nested inside a restrictive federal framework that no state law cancels. Border screening is the heaviest exposure — a Feb 2025 consular cable orders refusal where documents cast doubt on sex, permits a lifetime fraud-ineligibility finding, and has prompted advisories from eight-plus foreign governments; no real-time remedy is documented. Federal custody adds documented harm: immigration-detention abuse of trans detainees and a 2026 corrections policy mandating forced de-transition, reachable if a discrepancy escalates. A national order bars trans people from federally funded single-sex facilities even here. Offsetting: no trans-specific criminal offence, functioning courts that have enjoined orders, a sanctuary law expressly shielding travelling families seeking care, identity-based prison housing (last documented 2021), and a 'safest laws' band alongside rising recorded hostility.

entry_documents.exposure: Feb 2025 consular cable directs officers to refuse cases where document discrepancy casts reasonable doubt on sex, and to consider a lifetime fraud-ineligibility finding; X and non-assigned-sex markers no longer issued; trans travellers report passports blocked/confiscated; eight-plus governments issued travel advisories over identity-document and data rules.
entry_documents.protection: No documented categorical ban on trans visitors; the lifetime bar requires four elements, is never automatic, and has limited waivers; existing X-marker passports remain valid; challenge pending in national courts.
entry_documents.interaction: Document discrepancy → refusal or secondary screening → possible detention → federal custody rules govern, overriding the sub-unit's protective posture.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: In immigration custody transgender men reported forced-labour programmes, beatings, solitary confinement and severe sexual abuse. From 2026 the national corrections bureau adopted a policy mandating conversion therapy for trans inmates — short hair, hormone removal, substitute psychiatric drugs; reporting of trans prisoner numbers stopped in 2025; the earlier LGBTQ prison-protection order was rescinded.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: Sub-unit prison system documented as housing trans inmates by gender identity within general population and funding gender-affirming surgery (2015–2021 record); national courts have enjoined several orders and litigation functions.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: A border discrepancy or federal charge routes the visitor into federal/immigration custody, where the sub-unit's identity-based housing practice does not apply and the 2026 de-transition policy governs.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: The Jan 2025 executive order bars trans people from government-funded single-sex facilities nationwide, reaching federally funded buildings inside this sub-unit; nationally 21+ sub-units restrict facilities, 4 criminalise use, and a trans student was arrested and held 24 hours in a men's ward (March 2025, a different sub-unit).
federal_state_facilities.protection: July 2026 analysis places this sub-unit in the top protective-law band; no facility ban for this sub-unit is documented; documented identity-based prison housing.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: State protections do not reach federally funded facilities (federal buildings, federally funded terminals); a state 'no ban' status therefore does not remove the federal exposure.

care_services.exposure: Jan 2025 executive order frames minors' gender-affirming care as mutilation; summer 2025 DOJ subpoenas sought full records of under-19 patients from 20+ hospitals; national funding freeze, proposed Oct 2025 insurance rule, and closure of specialised LGBTQ youth services on the crisis lifeline.
care_services.protection: Sub-unit's Sept 2022 sanctuary law expressly shields families travelling here for a young person's hormones or puberty blockers from child-abuse investigations and criminal prosecution.
care_services.interaction: The state shield binds state investigators and prosecutors but does not immunise families or clinicians from federal subpoenas or federal charging authority.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: May 2026 counterterrorism strategy prioritises neutralising groups 'radically pro-transgender'; Dec 2025 DOJ reward memo invokes 'radical gender ideology' among violent-extremist viewpoints; Jan 2025 order directs law enforcement to investigate schools over 'gender ideology'; 2025 poll: 66% back ASAB on government documents.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: The same memo states rewards are not triggered by 'radical gender ideology' as a criterion and that counterterrorism powers will not target mere disagreement; national hate-crime statute covers gender identity; 2020 employment ruling in force.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Hostile official framing raises outing probability and deters help-seeking, but confers no independent arrest authority over a visitor.

minors_guardians.exposure: DOJ hospital-record subpoenas for under-19s; national order criminalising facilitation of a trans minor's social transition (aimed at teachers, with funding revocation); care restrictions and facility bans in schools; a trans minor's documents fall under the same entry-scrutiny regime.
minors_guardians.protection: Sub-unit sanctuary law expressly covers families who travel here for care and shields them from state abuse investigations and prosecution; documented as the first such sub-unit.
minors_guardians.interaction: For an adult travelling with a trans minor, the state shield is real but partial: it does not reach federal data demands, federal charging, or the border document regime.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: 198 anti-LGBTQ incidents recorded in this sub-unit in 2025 — highest raw count nationally, no population denominator; largest city shows a documented 'dramatic increase' in anti-LGBTQ hate-crime reports over the same period, coinciding with the governor platforming anti-trans figures.
street_violence_police_response.protection: National hate-crime statute covers gender identity; 2020 employment-discrimination ruling; sub-unit rated in the 'safest laws' band with a low recorded-incident count in a July 2026 analysis; no documented pattern of police hostility to trans people here.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Incident counts and law-enforcement hate-crime reports conflict with the protective-law rating; magnitude remains unresolved because neither figure is population-adjusted.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: The passport, executive-order and proposed-rule challenges are all unresolved; the passport restriction took effect in Nov 2025; no documented real-time remedy exists at the border, where officers act first and litigation follows; several exposures (prison housing currency, per-capita incident rates) are explicitly undetermined.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Functioning courts have blocked or enjoined several orders; a national civil-liberties union suit is live; a legal-aid organisation maintains an operative FAQ on document rules; national employment and hate-crime protections remain in force.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Remedies are retrospective — they can undo or restrain measures but cannot restore entry, prevent a border refusal, or stop a custody placement during the visit.

anchor_checks.comparison: Lower than 0.35-A: there is no categorical Visitor Conduct Register barring trans visitors — refusals are discrepancy-triggered, the lifetime bar is non-automatic with waivers, no trans-specific offence exists here, and courts are actively adjudicating challenges. Higher than it only in discretion: officers hold broad, unpublished real-time judgment over 'reasonable doubt on sex' with no effective in-country remedy, and several governments now advise trans citizens against travel.

Comparable overall, different shape. 0.45-D burdens daily life through registration and hotel reporting; this sub-unit documents no such visitor-registration regime, so everyday exposure is lower. But this jurisdiction adds sharper institutional harm: a directive refusal regime at entry plus documented immigration-custody abuse and a federal forced de-transition custody policy, giving a worse tail for equivalent probability.

Below 0.55-B. Its extended secondary screening, discretionary refusal and slow appeals map closely onto this border regime — but 0.55-B stays administrative, whereas here refusal can become a lifetime fraud finding, trans detainees document beatings and sexual abuse in immigration custody, and federal custody policy mandates de-transition. State-level sanctuary and identity-based prison housing soften only the sub-unit layer, not entry or federal custody.

Materially below 0.75-C: no trained, respectful inspection regime or written-reasons-and-compensation practice is documented; instead an affirmative instruction to refuse on sex doubt, a live lifetime-bar pathway, and foreign travel advisories. What 0.75-C has — brief detention ending in release, tribunal remedy, counsel access — is absent here for the border stage, though the sub-unit's protections approach that level for street, care and housing.

parsed.synthesis: The sub-unit operates genuine protective machinery — a sanctuary law that reaches travelling families seeking care, identity-based prison housing, a top protective-law band, functioning courts — but none of it binds the federal layers every visitor passes. Entry is governed by a consular instruction to refuse on perceived sex doubt, with a lifetime fraud finding as leverage and no real-time remedy; a discrepancy can escalate into immigration custody where abuse of trans detainees is documented, and into federal custody where a 2026 policy mandates de-transition. The federal facility bar applies even inside this protective sub-unit. Daily exposure here is moderated by state law yet coexists with rising recorded hostility, so protections lower street risk without neutralising border and custody risk.
